background: In approximately August 2021, hundreds of gigabytes of business data collated from public sources was obtained and later published to a popular hacking forum . Sourced from a customer of Bureau van Dijk's (BvD) "Orbis" product, the corpus of data released contained hundreds of millions of lines about corporations and individuals, including personal information such as names and dates of birth.

The data also included 28M unique email addresses along with physical addresses (presumedly corporate locations), phone numbers and job titles. There was no unauthorised access to BvD's systems, nor did the incident expose any of their or parent company's Moody's clients.
how: There was no unauthorised access to BvD's systems, nor did the incident expose any of their or parent company's Moody's clients.
outcome: 27,917,714 accounts are listed in this breach. This is a count of accounts, not necessarily individual people.
The reported exposed data includes Dates of birth, Email addresses, Job titles, Names, Phone numbers, Physical addresses.
editorial: Nobody in this file has a relationship with the company named at the top of it. Personal details were collated from public sources into Bureau van Dijk's Orbis product, Orbis was licensed to customers, and the leak came from one of those customers. Three hops between the person and the breach, and the person chose none of them.

That is the structural failure of the data broker economy rather than a lapse by anyone in particular. Aggregation is the entire product: a name in one register, a date of birth in a filing, a job title on a third site are individually public and individually useless, and combining them into a profile is what the customer is paying for.

Once assembled, the profile copies perfectly and ends up exactly as secure as the least careful licensee. The vendor can be faultless and the outcome identical. Which is why "sourced from public information" reassures less than it is meant to.

Nothing here can be withdrawn at source, because none of it was private to begin with, and there is no account to close, no consent to revoke, and no notification obligation to anyone whose dossier was compiled without their involvement. The exposure is the collation, and the collation is the business.

fields.name: Physical addresses
fields.why: Where someone actually lives. Combined with a name this moves the risk off the internet.

fields.name: Phone numbers
fields.why: Enables SIM-swap attacks against SMS two-factor codes, and puts the number on scam-call lists indefinitely.

fields.name: Dates of birth
fields.why: One of the three things call centres ask to verify identity, and it never changes.

fields.name: Names
fields.why: Turns an anonymous address into an identified person, which is what makes targeted phishing possible.

fields.name: Email addresses
fields.why: The address becomes a confirmed, active target, expect more phishing, better aimed.

fields.name: Job titles
fields.why: Identifies who has access to what, which is how targets for business email compromise are picked.

actions: Move two-factor authentication off SMS and onto an authenticator app, which a SIM swap cannot intercept.
Be sceptical of post and callers who already know your address, knowing it is no longer evidence of anything.
Expect better-aimed phishing. A message that already knows your name and where you have an account is the whole point of a breach like this.
breach.scale_line: That is roughly everyone in Australia.
